title: An optimizer is a way of walking a landscape, and the fair way to compare walkers is best-so-far against evaluations
summary: An objective function is a landscape. Gradient descent, Nelder-Mead and evolution strategies walk it in three different ways, each with a landscape it handles badly. Compare them by the best value found against the number of function evaluations on a log axis, and when two goals pull apart, report the Pareto front instead of one weighted number.

media.alt: Semi-log plot of best objective value so far against 200 evaluations for three optimizers, each a line with a shaded band. Optimizer A falls fastest to about 0.005, B to about 0.06, C only to about 0.2; the bands widen with the evaluation count.
media.caption: Reference render of plot class F7.1 with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery), not a project result.

source.note: Standard optimization theory. The figure is the design system's synthetic F7.1 render, so no project number is quoted. Every number in the derivation and the worked example was computed for this page and checked by script.

read_the_figure.question: Which optimizer reaches a lower objective value for the same number of function evaluations, and how much does that depend on the random seed?
read_the_figure.axes: x: number of objective evaluations, the real cost when each evaluation is a simulation. y: the best objective value found so far on a logarithmic scale, so equal vertical steps are equal factors.
look_at: Each line is a median over repeated runs and the band is the spread between runs. Overlapping bands mean the ranking is not established.
The curve can only go down or stay flat, because 'best so far' never gets worse. A flat stretch is a stall.
On a log axis a straight line is linear convergence: the slope is the logarithm of the factor gained per evaluation.
The start of every curve is the same only if every optimizer got the same starting point and budget.
read_the_figure.proves: If the band of one optimizer lies entirely below another's over the whole budget, that optimizer is better on this problem at this budget.
if_wrong: x axis labelled iterations: a gradient step, a simplex step and a population generation cost very different numbers of evaluations, so the comparison is unfair.
A single run per optimizer with no band: the picture shows luck as much as skill.
A linear y axis: all the information below the first few percent of the starting value is squashed into the bottom edge.
must_check: Log y axis and the value that counts as converged.
Same starting points and same budget for every optimizer.
A band or individual runs, with the number of seeds stated.

terms.meaning: The number that says how bad a design is. Optimization searches for the inputs that make it smallest.
The graph of f over its inputs, read as terrain: valleys are good, hills are bad, and the search is a walk across it.
The vector of slopes. It points straight uphill; its negative is the steepest way down.
The matrix of second derivatives: how curved the landscape is in each direction.
The ratio of the steepest to the flattest curvature of a valley. A long thin valley has a large one.
n+1 points in n dimensions (a triangle in 2D). Nelder-Mead moves, stretches and shrinks it across the landscape using function values only.
A population method: sample candidates from a Gaussian cloud, keep the best, move and reshape the cloud toward them. CMA-ES is the best-known version.
Design a dominates design b if a is no worse in every objective and strictly better in at least one.
The set of designs that nothing dominates: every one of them is the best possible trade-off for some preference.
The point on a front where a small gain in one objective starts to cost a lot in the other, usually the best compromise when no preference is given.

remember: Gradient descent: $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha\nabla f(x_k)$. It is stable only for $\alpha<2/\lambda_{\max}$.
On a quadratic valley its error shrinks by $(\kappa-1)/(\kappa+1)$ per step at best, so a large condition number means a very slow walk.
Nelder-Mead and evolution strategies need only values of $f$, no gradients: they survive noise and kinks, and they pay in evaluations.
Compare optimizers by best-so-far against evaluations, on a log axis, over several seeds.
$a$ dominates $b$ if it is no worse everywhere and better somewhere. The Pareto front is what is left when you delete every dominated design.
A weighted sum can only reach the convex part of a front. The epsilon-constraint method reaches all of it.

understand.title: Easy: a landscape and the three ways to walk it
understand.text: Picture a mountain range with fog. Gradient descent feels the slope under its feet and steps downhill, so it needs the slope. Nelder-Mead holds a small triangle, finds the worst corner and flips it over the best side, so it needs only heights. An evolution strategy throws a handful of darts around its current guess, notices which landed lowest and moves the whole cloud that way, so it also needs only heights, and it reshapes the cloud so that it becomes long in the direction of the valley. Same landscape, three different kinds of information used.

understand.title: Medium: why the same problem can be easy for one walker and hopeless for another
understand.text: On a smooth bowl with round contours, gradient descent walks straight to the bottom. On a long curved valley such as Rosenbrock's banana, the gradient points across the narrow valley, not along it, so the walker zig-zags between the walls. The curvature ratio along to across is the condition number, and for Rosenbrock's valley floor it is about 2500. Rastrigin's surface is a bowl covered in egg-box dimples: every dimple traps a gradient walker, while a population with a wide enough cloud steps over the dimples. Himmelblau's surface has four equal minima: which one you reach depends on where you start, and a single run says nothing about the others.

understand.title: Hard: what 'CMA-ES' does in one sentence
understand.text: Sample $\lambda$ points from $\mathcal N(\mathbf m,\sigma^2C)$, rank them by $f$, move the mean to a weighted average of the best $\mu$, and rebuild the covariance $C$ from the steps that were selected. Because selection keeps the points that fell toward the valley, the selected steps are long along the valley and short across it, so the new $C$ is a thin ellipse aligned with the contour lines. The method learns the shape of the landscape from rankings alone. Step 5 of the derivation checks that effect numerically.

understand.title: Hardest: two objectives, no single best
understand.text: With a cost and a loss, a design that wins on cost may lose on loss, so there is no single best design, only a set of undominated ones: the Pareto front. A weighted sum $w_1f_1+w_2f_2$ turns the problem back into one objective, but each choice of weights finds only a point where a straight line touches the front from outside. If the front bends the wrong way (is concave), no weights ever select an interior point. The epsilon-constraint method minimises one objective while holding the other below a bound, and moving the bound walks along the whole front. Steps 7 and 8 prove this on a small example.

steps.title: The landscape and the descent rule
steps.note: From a point, the negative gradient is the direction in which f falls fastest locally; alpha is how far to walk before looking again. Atlas S13 example 1 draws this climb (downhill is the same walk with the sign flipped).

steps.title: On a quadratic valley the error is multiplied each step
steps.note: Any smooth minimum looks like this quadratic nearby, with H the Hessian there. Each eigen-direction of H shrinks by the factor 1 - alpha lambda_i, so the steepest direction sets the largest safe step. Checked numerically: with alpha 1.9 over lambda_max the error decays, with 2.1 over lambda_max it explodes.

steps.title: The best fixed step and the slow rate it still gives
steps.note: The step that balances the steepest and the flattest direction makes the two factors 1 - alpha lambda_min and alpha lambda_max - 1 equal in size. If kappa is 1 the error vanishes in one step; if kappa is large, rho is close to 1 and every step gains almost nothing. Verified symbolically and by running the iteration.

steps.title: Rosenbrock's valley floor has a large condition number
steps.note: The gradient at (1,1) is zero and the Hessian is computed symbolically; its eigenvalues were checked numerically. A banana valley is just a very anisotropic bowl near the minimum (Rosenbrock 1960 introduced the function as a test).

steps.title: Nelder-Mead: reflect the worst vertex through the centroid
steps.note: Only the ordering of f at the n+1 vertices is used. Reflection moves the simplex away from the worst point; expansion speeds it up in a good direction, contraction slows it down when the move did not help, and shrink restarts small around the best vertex. On Rosenbrock from (-1.2, 1) the standard algorithm reached (1, 1) in 219 evaluations in this check.

steps.title: Evolution strategy: selection reshapes the cloud
steps.tex: y_i\sim\mathcal N(0,C),\quad x_i=m+\sigma y_i,\qquad m'=\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}w_i\,x_{(i)},\qquad C'=(1-c)\,C+c\sum_{i=1}^{\mu}w_i\,y_{(i)}y_{(i)}^{\mathsf T}
steps.note: x(i) is the i-th best of the lambda samples. Numerical check: for f = (x1^2 + 100 x2^2)/2 and a round cloud, the best quarter of 200,000 samples has a variance ratio of about 26 to 1 between the flat and the steep direction, so the selected steps already point along the valley. Repeating this each generation is how the shape is learned from rankings alone.

steps.title: Why best-so-far against evaluations on a log axis is fair
steps.tex: f_{\text{best}}(N)=\min_{j\le N}f(x_j),\qquad f_{\text{best}}(N)\approx C\rho^{\,N}\ \Rightarrow\ \log f_{\text{best}}=\log C+N\log\rho
steps.note: N counts evaluations, because that is the cost. One gradient step costs n+1 evaluations if the gradient is made by finite differences, one evolution generation costs lambda, one Nelder-Mead step costs one or two: iterations are not comparable. The minimum over everything tried so far is monotone, and on a log y axis linear convergence is a straight line whose slope is log rho.

steps.title: Pareto dominance and the knee
steps.tex: a\prec b\iff f_i(a)\le f_i(b)\ \forall i\ \text{and}\ f_j(a)<f_j(b)\ \text{for some }j;\qquad f_1=x^2,\ f_2=(x-2)^2,\ x\in[0,2]:\ \text{knee at }x=1
steps.note: Here the front is x between 0 and 2. Knee defined as the point farthest from the straight line through the two extreme designs (0, 4) and (4, 0), which is the line f1 + f2 = 4: the distance is proportional to 4 - f1 - f2 = 4x - 2x^2, largest at x = 1, giving (1, 1). Verified symbolically.

steps.title: Weighted sum misses concave fronts; epsilon-constraint does not
steps.tex: f_1=t,\ f_2=1-t^2,\ t\in[0,1]:\quad w_1t+w_2(1-t^2)\ \text{is concave in }t\Rightarrow\ \min\text{ at }t=0\text{ or }1;\qquad \min f_1\ \text{s.t. } f_2\le\varepsilon\ \Rightarrow\ t=\sqrt{1-\varepsilon}
steps.note: A concave function on an interval is smallest at an end, so for every choice of weights the weighted sum returns an extreme design and never an interior one. Fixing f2 below epsilon instead returns t = sqrt(1 - epsilon), for example t = 0.6 for epsilon = 0.64. Checked numerically over weights 0.1, 0.5 and 0.9.

worked.title: How many gradient steps does Rosenbrock's valley floor cost?
worked.problem: Near the minimum (1, 1) the Hessian of Rosenbrock's function has eigenvalues 0.3994 and 1001.6. Using the best fixed step, how many gradient-descent steps are needed to shrink the error by a factor of $10^{6}$, and why is that a bad deal compared with 219 Nelder-Mead evaluations?
worked.answer: About 17,300 gradient steps (the iteration itself, run on the quadratic with alpha = 0.001996, took 17,325). Each step also needs a gradient, 3 evaluations of f in 2D by finite differences, so more than 50,000 evaluations against 219 for Nelder-Mead from (-1.2, 1) in this check. Gradient descent is not bad in general; this valley is simply long and thin, which is the one case it is worst at, and a method that learns the valley's shape wins by orders of magnitude.

analyze.q: On the optimizer-race plot the best curve of the three is also the widest band. What can you conclude about its ranking at 200 evaluations, and what would you do to be sure?
analyze.hint: Look at whether the bands overlap at the right edge; more seeds narrow the median's uncertainty.

analyze.q: Rastrigin's surface has a global minimum surrounded by many local ones. Why does a gradient method started at random almost always fail on it, and what property of an evolution strategy's population helps?
analyze.hint: Think about the cloud's width compared with the spacing between dimples.

analyze.q: Himmelblau's function has four equal minima. If you run 20 starts and a method ends at all four, is that a failure of the method? What changes if you needed the one with the smallest cost?
analyze.hint: Four equal minima means the answer is not unique; only multi-start tells you about the others.

evaluate.q: A paper compares a gradient method and a population method by the number of iterations and shows the gradient method winning. What is wrong with the comparison, and how would you repair it?
evaluate.hint: Cost per iteration is not the same; how many evaluations did each iteration use, and how were the gradients obtained?

evaluate.q: A weighted sum with equal weights picked an extreme design and the team concluded the objectives do not conflict. What else could explain that result?
evaluate.hint: Concave fronts give extremes for every weight; check with epsilon-constraint or a front plot.

create: Design a fair optimizer race for a simulation where one evaluation takes ten minutes: budget, number of seeds, what to plot, and what you would report if two methods' bands overlap.
Sketch a Pareto plot for cost against loss that makes the knee visible without a legend: which annotations and which axes would you use, and would you use log scales?
A robust or scale-balanced objective combines errors across quantities that differ by orders of magnitude. How would you check that it is not hiding a poor fit on the smallest quantity?

checks.q: Why does gradient descent zig-zag in a long thin valley?
checks.hint: Where does the negative gradient point on the wall of a valley, compared with the direction along the valley floor?
checks.answer: The gradient is perpendicular to the contour lines. On the sides of a narrow valley the contours run along the valley, so the gradient points across it, toward the opposite wall, and each step overshoots the floor and lands higher up the other side. The component along the valley is tiny because the floor is almost flat, so progress along it is slow. The ratio of curvatures, the condition number, measures how bad this is.

checks.q: A valley has curvature eigenvalues 1 and 100. What is the best fixed step, the contraction factor per step and the number of steps to gain a factor of $10^{3}$?
On a log-y race plot, optimizer A is a straight line and optimizer B flattens out after 100 evaluations. What does each shape mean?
checks.hint: A straight line on a log axis is a constant factor per evaluation.
checks.answer: A converges at a constant rate: each evaluation multiplies the best value by the same factor. B made quick early progress and then stalled: a local minimum, a collapsed step size or a noise floor. Which of these it is cannot be read from the curve; look at the trajectory (class F7.2) or the step size.

checks.q: Which of these designs on (cost, loss) is dominated: A(1, 9), B(2, 5), C(3, 6), D(4, 3), E(5, 4)? Which of the others would you call the knee?
checks.hint: A design is dominated if another one is no worse in both objectives.
checks.answer: C is dominated by B (2 is less than 3 and 5 is less than 6), and E is dominated by D (4 is less than 5 and 3 is less than 4). A, B and D remain. For A, B, D the farthest from the line through the extremes A(1, 9) and D(4, 3) is B, so B is the knee: the move from A to B buys a big loss reduction for a small cost increase, while B to D costs more for less.

checks.q: Your simulation is expensive and noisy. Which optimizer family would you start with, how would you set up the comparison, and what is the first thing you would plot?
checks.hint: No gradients and no money for many evaluations: think about what the budget and the noise allow.
checks.answer: A derivative-free population method such as an evolution strategy (or Nelder-Mead for a small number of parameters) because gradients by finite differences are corrupted by noise and cost n + 1 evaluations each. Fix the budget, use the same starting points and 5 to 20 seeds, and plot best-so-far against evaluations on a log axis with a band, which shows both speed and reliability. Then plot the trajectory in the parameters to see whether the method explored or stalled.
